parsed.explanation: The operative regime is split: a hostile national layer governs every stage the traveller actually passes through — passport/visa markers restricted to birth sex, border officers instructed to refuse cases with document discrepancy and to consider lifetime fraud ineligibility, and immigration custody where transgender detainees report forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and sexual abuse. These are the combined regime's heaviest features and the division's protections do not reach them. Once inside, the division is genuinely protective: public-accommodations and hate-crime coverage, a 2023 shield law for care, gender-neutral single-occupancy restrooms, and a 'Most Protective' ranking. But a subnational statute does not cancel federal entry screening, federal facilities or federal custody. Exposure is discretionary rather than automatic, and no credible path to execution exists, so this sits at the top of the Elevated band rather than in High Risk.

entry_documents.exposure: National rules bar X markers and self-selected gender on passports/visas; officers must refuse cases where documents cast doubt on sex and may consider a permanent fraud ineligibility finding; travellers report passports confiscated or blocked and some stranded abroad.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiry; the passport policy is under litigation; a legal-aid FAQ tracks the rules.
entry_documents.interaction: Division protections (shield law, marker-change procedures) do not touch national passport or visa adjudication; the traveller carries a home-issued passport and meets the national rule at the port of entry.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Immigration custody: transgender men report forced-labour programmes, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse; national prison policy since 2026 imposes hair-cutting, hormone withdrawal and psychiatric substitution; the corrections bureau stopped reporting transgender prisoner counts in 2025.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Consular notification and limited waiver possibilities for fraud findings exist on paper; national prison LGBTQ protections were rescinded.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A document discrepancy at the border can escalate into immigration detention, where the documented harms sit wholly in the national system the division cannot regulate.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National executive order bars transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities matching identity; facility bans operate in roughly 21 states/territories, 4 with criminal exposure.
federal_state_facilities.protection: This division has gender-neutral single-occupancy restrooms by statute and municipal self-identification rules for bathroom access; it has no facility ban.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Inside the division, facilities are largely safe; national buildings and national-funded facilities remain governed by the national exclusion, and a traveller transiting other states/territories meets their bans.

care_services.exposure: National orders describe minor gender-affirming care as mutilation, restrict funding and threaten prosecution of teachers facilitating social transition; national health rules proposed to bar reimbursement for under-18 care.
care_services.protection: Division shield law (2023) protects patients and providers, including visitors from states where care is banned; conversion-therapy ban for minors; public insurance covers surgery for adults 21+.
care_services.interaction: Shield law works only within the division and only against other states' bans; national funding restrictions, subpoenas of hospital records and national insurance rules still reach visitors using nationally regulated services.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National counterterrorism strategy (May 2026) lists 'radically pro-transgender' groups among priorities for rapid neutralization; a justice-department reward memorandum invokes 'radical gender ideology'; national agencies purged gender terms and revoked LGBT research grants.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Strategy text disclaims targeting mere disagreement; national hate-crime statute covers gender identity; division hate-crime enhancements since 2016 and unanimous repeal of gay/trans panic defence.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Rhetoric is national and shapes border and law-enforcement discretion; division police and prosecutors operate under protective state law but cannot bind national agencies.

minors_guardians.exposure: National executive order directs law enforcement to investigate schools promoting 'gender ideology' and to prosecute teachers who use a trans minor's preferred name or pronouns; 27 states ban youth care; a trans student was arrested in a capitol restroom under a state bathroom law.
minors_guardians.protection: Division bans conversion therapy on minors, mandates school bullying protections and a 2019 executive order on names, pronouns and dress codes; shield law covers visiting minors' care.
minors_guardians.interaction: A parent travelling with a trans minor crosses a national border regime that may scrutinise documents and a national school-prosecution policy, while the division's school protections begin only after entry.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: National risk assessment flags four 'Do Not Travel' states for trans people; anti-trans bills and facility enforcement create hostile local climates in parts of the country; bias statutes cover gender identity in only 23 states.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Division has banned discrimination in employment, housing, credit and public accommodations since 2006, extended hate-crime penalties to gender identity in 2016, and ranks in the 'Most Protective' tier.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Street risk is highly jurisdiction-dependent; the traveller is well protected in this division but unprotected in much of the surrounding country she may transit.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Entry refusals and fraud findings have limited waiver routes and slow review; national-court challenges to passport and executive-order policy remain unresolved; whether the division shield law withstands out-of-state subpoenas is undocumented.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Active national litigation by a civil-liberties union; some orders enjoined; division courts, human-rights commissions and hate-crime enforcement operate.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies exist but are largely post-hoc and national; at the border the traveller has no effective real-time recourse, and division remedies cannot reach a national detention facility.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar in that the primary harm at the national layer is exclusion, refusal and humiliation at the border rather than execution; worse because this regime also documents immigration-custody beatings and sexual abuse and a possible lifetime fraud ineligibility, and better because a large protective subnational regime covers daily life once admitted.

Both feature discretionary secondary screening triggered by document/presentation mismatch, administrative rather than criminal outcomes, and appeals that rarely reverse decisions. This case has stronger documented custodial harm after referral and a hostile national threat-framing layer, but a far more protective internal jurisdiction, which roughly nets out below that anchor.

That anchor has trained border officers and a tribunal that reliably releases and compensates. Here the border is the weak point: officers are instructed to refuse discrepant cases, custody abuse is documented, and division protections expressly do not reach entry or national custody, so the case sits materially lower.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller meets the national regime first and last: passport and visa adjudication, border screening, possible immigration detention and any national custody are governed by rules the division cannot alter, and those rules include refusal for document discrepancy, a possible lifetime fraud finding, and documented abuse in immigration custody. Between those points she is in one of the most protective divisions in the country, with public-accommodations law, hate-crime coverage, a care shield law and gender-neutral restrooms. Because the harshest operative rule governs how the visit is experienced, the division's protections raise the score above the national line but cannot lift it into Reduced Risk.
